lesson_title: Why the Pot Sticks at One Hundred
hook_text: Your stove is on full and the thermometer refuses to move. Where is all that energy going?
clip_script: Put a pot of water on the stove with a thermometer in it. Forty, sixty, eighty, ninety-nine, one hundred — and then it stops. The stove is still on full, the electricity is still costing you money, and the reading will not budge past one hundred until the pot is nearly empty. So where is the energy going? Not into making the particles faster. Temperature just measures how hard the particles jiggle on average, and if the thermometer is not moving, the jiggling is not increasing. The energy is doing a completely different job: it is pulling the particles apart. Water particles hold onto each other, and turning liquid into steam means breaking every one of those grips. Think of it as paying off a debt before you can save — every joule goes to the debt collector, the forces holding the particles together, and only once the debt is settled does the balance start climbing again. Same thing at the bottom: ice sticks at zero as slush until the last piece is gone. That's why a steam burn is so vicious — the steam dumps every joule of that separation energy back into your skin.
visual_style: Kitchen close-up: a rolling pot with a thermometer frozen at 100, then a cutaway into jiggling particles being prised apart one grip at a time, ending on a temperature-time staircase drawing itself with two flat steps.
pacing: Slow suspense on the stuck thermometer, quick particle reveal, calm landing on the graph.
